h1: Beer etiquette in pubs abroad from rounds to tipping
title: Beer Etiquette in Pubs Abroad | Craft Beer School
desc: How ordering, rounds, toasts and tipping work in pubs and beer halls in the UK, Germany, Belgium, the Czech Republic, the US and Japan.
teaser: Order at the bar or wait for the waiter? Tip or round up? A short guide to not looking lost in a pub abroad.
standfirst: Every beer culture has rules nobody writes down. Get them wrong and you wait twenty minutes for a beer that was never coming. Here is how ordering, rounds and tipping work in six countries Indian beer lovers visit most.
sections: Pub rules differ more than the beer does

In most Indian brewpubs a server takes your order at the table and the bill arrives at the end. That habit travels badly. In a British pub nobody will come to your table. In a Czech beer hall a fresh half litre lands in front of you before you have asked. In Tokyo nobody drinks until the whole table has raised a glass.

None of this is complicated once you know it. The rules below are the broad norms. Local habits vary by city and by venue, so watch what the regulars do for two minutes before you move.
Britain and Ireland: order at the bar and buy your round

Walk to the bar, catch the bartender's eye and order. Pay as you go. Draught beer comes in pints (568 ml) or halves. A third of a pint is common at craft bars for strong beers.

Groups drink in rounds. One person buys for everyone, then the next person buys the next round. Leaving before your turn is noticed. If the group is large or you are drinking slowly, it is fine to say you will sit this round out and buy your own.

Tipping at the bar is not expected. Regulars sometimes say "and one for yourself", which lets the bartender add the price of a drink to the bill. Table service in a gastropub is different: a service charge of around 10 to 12.5% is often added to the bill.
Germany and the Czech Republic: the waiter keeps the count

In a German beer hall or a Czech pub you sit down and a server comes to you. In Cologne the Kölsch server keeps replacing your small 200 ml glass until you put your beer mat on top of it. In Prague and Pilsen a fresh half litre often arrives the moment your glass is nearly empty. Your tally is marked on a slip of paper or on the beer mat.

Paying is done at the table. Tipping is usually a matter of rounding up, often to about 5 to 10% more. Tell the server the total you want to pay as you hand over the money rather than leaving coins on the table.

Toasting matters. Look the person in the eye as you clink glasses. "Prost" in Germany, "Na zdraví" in the Czech Republic.
Belgium: every beer has its own glass

Belgian cafés usually serve at the table. The detail visitors notice is the glassware. Many Belgian beers have a branded glass and bars try hard to use the right one. A strong Tripel in a chalice, a Gueuze in a tall tumbler. Our glassware guide explains why shape changes what you smell.

Belgian beers also run strong. A Tripel is often around 8 to 9% ABV, so a 330 ml bottle carries more alcohol than a British pint of bitter. Pace accordingly. Tipping is modest: rounding up is enough in most cafés.
The United States: tip every drink

American bars are the opposite of British ones on tipping. Staff wages assume tips, so you are expected to tip. At the bar the common habit is about one dollar per beer. At a table, 15 to 20% of the bill is normal.

A US pint is 16 US fluid ounces, about 473 ml, smaller than a British pint. Taprooms often sell tasting flights of four or five small pours, which is the best way to try a brewery's range without drinking three full pints. Carry photo ID. Bars check it, whatever your age looks like.
Japan: wait for kanpai and pour for others

In Japan the first round arrives together and nobody drinks until someone says "kanpai". After that, you pour for the people around you and they pour for you. Topping up your own glass is a small social miss. Hold your glass up a little when someone pours for you.

Tipping is not part of the culture and can cause awkwardness. Many izakayas add a small seating charge that comes with a tiny dish of food. That is normal, not a mistake on the bill.

Whatever the country, the same courtesy travels: drink at your own pace, order water without embarrassment and never drive after drinking. Bars in every country on this list will serve you a glass of water. Many also sell alcohol free beer now.

Before your next trip, look up two phrases in the local language: how to say cheers and how to ask for the bill. Then spend your first two minutes in the bar watching where people order and how they pay.
faqs: Do you tip in British pubs?
Not at the bar. Some regulars offer the bartender a drink instead. Table service restaurants often add a service charge of around 10 to 12.5%.
How much should I tip for a beer in the US?
About one dollar per beer at the bar is common. At a table, 15 to 20% of the bill is normal.
What does a beer mat on top of a glass mean in Germany?
In Cologne it tells the Kölsch server you have finished and do not want another glass.
It is not expected and can cause confusion. Polite thanks is enough.
